newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bullish Vereinsbank plays down takeover talk.
newsitem.headline: Bullish Vereinsbank plays down takeover talk.

text.p: Germany's Bayerische Vereinsbank AG, much touted as a takeover candidate, on Thursday played down talk of an acquisition war in German banking while giving a bullish outlook for 1997 profits on Thursday.

In an unusually forthright declaration, Vereinsbank chairman Albrecht Schmidt said cost, capital and reputation issues meant unfriendly bids on the lines of steel and engineering firm Krupp's shock assault on rival Thyssen AG this week were unworkable for banks.
While acknowledging the need for consolidation in the overcrowded sector, Schmidt said: "I consider an unfriendly takeover of a (German) bank to be impossible."

Schmidt said the Bavarian mortgage specialist should post a "substantial increase" in operating profit this year after strong interest and commission income boosted its operating income by 18.4 percent to 1.6 billion marks ($949 million) in 1996.
"Business in the first two months was excellent," he said, adding that Vereinsbank's well-distributed profit base gave it "a certain immunity" from unpleasant economic shocks.

Interest income from mortgage and banking business looked set to rise again this year, Schmidt said, and an expansion of trading activities should lead to higher own-account trading income, which dropped six percent to 254 million marks in 1996.
"With four percent growth in the global economy and a slight economic recovery in Germany ... I am optimistic for Vereinsbank's future," Schmidt said.

But Schmidt refused to be drawn on the various models for a restructured German banking scene which have been bandied about in the past year amid a flurry of speculation that a major upheaval was coming in the industry.
"I can only repeat what I have said before, we are keeping our eyes open," he said.
Vereinsbank has been at the centre of takeover speculation after market leader Deutsche Bank AG last year revealed it had built up a 5.2 percent stake in its Bavarian rival.

While Vereinsbank is generally believed to oppose a takeover by Deutsche, there has been much talk of a "Bavarian solution", involving some alliance with fellow mortgage lender Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG.
"We have a high banking density here in Germany and that is one of the weaknesses of the system," Schmidt said.
"But the decisive factor is profile. Too many are plain vanilla. We believe that we have a good profile -- people know what Vereinsbank stands for," he added.

Schmidt said a hostile takeover was impossible in German banks precisely for the profile reason, which would be lost if a takeover were forced on a bank since staff would not co-operate with a new owner.
In addition, an unfriendly takeover would eat up far too much capital, raising serious problems for a bank to maintain the core capital ratios demanded by law. That, he said, would be "fatal".

Schmidt also said Vereinsbank needed to work on bringing its profitability up to international standards. Net return on own capital rose to 8.6 percent in 1996 from 7.1 percent but remains firmly below a target of 11 percent.
Net profit for 1996, which had already been heralded in broad terms, advanced 32.3 percent to 869 million marks. Earnings per share rose to 2.83 marks from 2.52 marks.

But Schmidt said the Bavarian bank's profit distribution -- 31 percent from treasury business, 32 percent from corporate clients and 24 percent from retail banking -- should protect it from unpleasant shocks.

Detailing earnings by segment for the first time in preparation for a switch to International Accounting Standards, Schmidt said mortgage business accounted for 57 percent of operating profit and regular banking for 43 percent.

The bank's share price, which soared 45 percent in 1996 on merger speculation and closed bourse trade on Thursday 10 pfennigs lower at 61.80 marks, did not yet match the basic value of Vereinsbank and had further to go, Schmidt said. --Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.686 German Marks)
